[Project overview]{.eyebrow}

::: {.lead}
Evolutionary genetic theory for how coevolution between hosts and their
symbionts affects co-transmission of host and symbiont genomes.
:::

We developed population genetic models and computer simulations to investigate
the evolution of symbiont transmission. Without stochastic forces like mutation,
the conditions favoring vertical transmission of an obligate symbiont turn out
to be restrictive. This theoretical work shows that intimate host-symbiont
coevolution requires a high degree of specificity in the fitness interactions
between both players.

A companion result shows that antagonistic host-pathogen interactions generate
both spatial and temporal fluctuations in fitness, and therefore favor increased
dispersal rates. Under certain conditions, where interactions are strong, there
is continuous evolutionary escalation in dispersal rates, which helps explain
the ubiquity of dispersal in nature. The long-term evolution of dispersal
described by the model provides an understanding of the empirical evidence of
local adaptation necessary for host-parasite interactions to drive the evolution
of host and pathogen dispersal.
